\chapter{Which One: the Ordinals, Said and Written}
\label{ch:ru-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first, second and third, build the ordinal of any number I can count to, and read and write an ordinal as a figure with its ending hyphenated on.}

Two forms outside the pattern, one adjective ending for everything above them, and the written 1-y whose letters after the hyphen are the agreement rather than decoration.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pérvyy]{\ru{первый} — first}

\label{lesson:RU-C26-pervyy}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, say \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} and \textbf{\ru{сто}}, say \textbf{\ru{один}} and its root, and say what a number still does to the noun after it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{первый}} — \emph{pérvyy} — \textbf{first}
\end{quote}

Counting says \emph{how many}. Ordering says \emph{which one} — a floor number, a date, a queue, a chapter heading — and twelve numbers do not give you one of them.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{первый}} is not built from \textbf{\ru{один}}. It goes back to Indo-European *\emph{per-}, \textquotedblleft{}forward, in front,\textquotedblright{} which is also behind English \textbf{fore}, \textbf{before} and \textbf{former} — and behind \textbf{first} itself, which is \emph{fore} with a superlative ending on it.

So Russian and English break in the same place and for the same reason: the word for \emph{first} means \emph{foremost} in both, and neither is built from the word for \emph{one}. The series comes into line at \emph{second}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{первый}} — first
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ru{один}} counts, \textbf{\ru{первый}} orders
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{первый}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{per-} $\to$ English \textbf{fore}, \textbf{first}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D0\%BF\%D0\%B5\%D1\%80\%D0\%B2\%D1\%8B\%D0\%B9}{Wiktionary: \ru{первый}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vtoróy trétiy]{\ru{второй} and \ru{третий} — second, third, and the ending above them}

\label{lesson:RU-C26-vtoroy-tretiy}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{первый}} and why it is not built from \textbf{\ru{один}}. Then say \textbf{\ru{три}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — two words and an ending}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{второй}} — \emph{vtoróy} — \textbf{second}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{третий}} — \emph{trétiy} — \textbf{third}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ru{три}} is audible whole inside \textbf{\ru{третий}}. And from four upward the pattern settles completely: the ordinal is \textbf{the plain number with an adjective ending on it} — \textbf{\ru{четвёртый}}, fourth; \textbf{\ru{пятый}}, fifth; \textbf{\ru{десятый}}, tenth.

That is worth saying plainly, because it means the reader who has twelve cardinals has twelve ordinals as soon as they have one ending, with only \textbf{\ru{первый}} and \textbf{\ru{второй}} outside it.

Russian ordinals are adjectives, and that carries a debt as well as a rule: an adjective changes its ending to agree with what it describes, and this book has not taught an adjective yet. So the forms here are the ones a masculine noun takes, and agreeing them with anything else is an adjective chapter rather than a numeral one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{второй}} — second; \textbf{\ru{третий}} — third
  \item \emph{Hear:} \textbf{\ru{три}} inside \textbf{\ru{третий}}
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{\ru{четыре}} $\to$ \textbf{\ru{четвёртый}}; \textbf{\ru{десять}} $\to$ \textbf{\ru{десятый}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D0\%B2\%D1\%82\%D0\%BE\%D1\%80\%D0\%BE\%D0\%B9}{Wiktionary: \ru{второй}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pérvyy]{1-\ru{й} — writing an ordinal as a figure}

\label{lesson:RU-W26-ordinal-hyphen}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{первый}} and \textbf{\ru{второй}}, then build \textbf{\ru{пятый}} from \textbf{\ru{пять}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the figure and its ending}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{1-\ru{й}} — \emph{pérvyy} — first  \textbf{2-\ru{е}} — \emph{vtoróye} — second
\end{quote}

A Russian ordinal written as a figure carries the tail of its own ending after a hyphen. \textbf{1-\ru{й}} is \textbf{\ru{первый}} with everything but the last letter replaced by the figure; \textbf{2-\ru{е}} is \textbf{\ru{второе}} in the same way.

This is not decoration. Ordinals are adjectives, so the ending is the agreement — change what is being ordered and the letters after the hyphen change with it. That is why the figure alone will not do, and why an English reader who writes \textbf{1st} for all of them is losing information the Russian page is carrying.

The hyphen is the short dash this book taught among its punctuation, not the long dash that stands for a missing verb.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{1-\ru{й}}, \textbf{2-\ru{е}}, \textbf{3-\ru{й}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} each aloud as the full word
  \item \emph{Say it:} why the letters after the hyphen are not always the same
\end{itemize}

Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — which one, said and written}

\label{lesson:RU-C26-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, say \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} and \textbf{\ru{сто}}, and name the side of the family Russian is on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Say \textbf{\ru{первый}, \ru{второй}, \ru{третий}} in order, then out of order.
  \item \textbf{Build}, do not recall: fourth, fifth, tenth, twentieth.
  \item Write \textbf{1-\ru{й}}, \textbf{2-\ru{е}}, \textbf{3-\ru{й}} and read each aloud as a full word.
  \item Say which two of the series are not built from their numbers, and what English does in the same place.
  \item Count one to ten, say \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} and \textbf{\ru{сто}}, and say what a number still does to the noun after it that this book has not taught.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Close the numeral slice}

\label{lesson:RU-R26-close}



\begin{quote}
Say the first three ordinals, count one to five, and ask \textbf{\ru{сколько}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Everything this slice added, with nothing in front of you.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Count aloud one to ten, then say \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} and \textbf{\ru{сто}}.
  \item Write all twelve from dictation, shuffled.
  \item Say the first three ordinals, build three more, and write \textbf{1-\ru{й}} and \textbf{2-\ru{е}}.
  \item Say the English cousin of each of the ten cardinals. Every one has one.
  \item Say the two pairs that shaped each other — \textbf{\ru{семь} / \ru{восемь}}, \textbf{\ru{девять} / \ru{десять}} — and which side of the centum/satem split \textbf{\ru{сто}} puts Russian on.
  \item Say the one thing these numbers still cannot do, and which chapter owes it.
\end{enumerate}

Then say what the whole slice cost the hand: \textbf{no new Cyrillic letter at all.}
